pattern.task_title: Fill placeholders in a provided template
pattern.task_description: Given a template with marked placeholders, fill each placeholder while preserving the template formatting.
pattern.naive_request: I am going to provide a template for your output. Everything in all caps is a placeholder. Any time that you generate text, try to fit it into one of the placeholders that I list. Please preserve the formatting and overall template that I provide at https://myapi.com/NAME/profile/JOB
pattern.task_material:
Template: https://myapi.com/NAME/profile/JOB
Placeholder NAME: a realistic full name
Placeholder JOB: a realistic job title
pattern.role: You are a template-filling assistant who populates marked placeholders while preserving all surrounding formatting.
pattern.context: The output will be consumed by an automated system, so structural consistency is critical. Only replace the explicit placeholders.
instructions: Identify all placeholders (text in ALL CAPS) in the template.
Replace each placeholder with appropriate content.
Preserve all non-placeholder text and formatting exactly.
If a placeholder cannot be filled, flag it rather than guessing.
pattern.technique: Use schema-constrained formatting: identify each placeholder, substitute content, and verify the output preserves the original structure.
pattern.output: Return the filled template with placeholders replaced and all other text preserved.
pattern.reference_notes: A strong answer replaces NAME and JOB with realistic values while keeping the URL structure intact.
pattern.source_paper_title: A Prompt Pattern Catalog to Enhance Prompt Engineering with ChatGPT

llm_assessment.justification: All three runs share the same high-level behavior of not completing the template directly and instead asking the user to paste it, but they are not functionally identical. Runs 1 and 2 provide concrete replacement values for NAME and JOB, while Run 3 does not provide actual values and only describes what it would do after receiving more input. For reproducibility research, that difference changes how usable the outputs are for the stated task.
material_differences: Run 1 provides specific placeholder values: 'Jordan Mitchell' and 'Product Marketing Manager'.
Run 2 provides different specific placeholder values: 'Maya Richardson' and 'Senior Product Manager'.
Run 3 does not provide any concrete NAME/JOB replacements at all; it only asks for constraints and says it will fill them later.
Runs 1 and 2 partially satisfy the task by offering realistic values, whereas Run 3 does not materially advance the template filling task.

llm_assessment.justification: All three outputs satisfy the task in the same way: each replaces NAME and JOB with plausible values while preserving the required URL structure (`https://myapi.com/{NAME}/profile/{JOB}`). The differences are only in the specific chosen names and job titles, which do not change the function or validity of the response for research purposes.

Yes. All three runs complete the same template by replacing NAME and JOB with plausible, realistic values while preserving the original URL structure, which matches the task requirement. The differences are in the specific values chosen, and Run 3 adds brief explanatory text, but all outputs satisfy the task in materially the same way.
material_differences: Run 3 includes extra explanatory text (placeholder identification, substitutions, and verification) before the final filled URL, while Runs 1 and 2 provide only the completed URL.
